tagline: Up to Lemhi Pass, and more mountains than Lewis bargained for.
intro: From the Tendoy store on Idaho 28, at about 4,800 feet, the byway follows the Lemhi back road through the valley, turns up the Warm Springs Wood Road into the Beaverhead Mountains, contours near the Continental Divide to Lemhi Pass at 7,373 feet, and comes back down Agency Creek to where it started. It is 36 miles of single-lane gravel, with no guardrails on the exposed slopes.

Meriwether Lewis topped the pass on August 12, 1805, expecting to leave the Rockies behind, and saw immense ranges still to the west with snow on their tops. That night his party camped at a spring below and ate a piece of salt pork that had come with them from Illinois.

moments.title: Flag Unfurling Monument
moments.text: Here Lewis's advance party showed the Stars and Stripes to the Lemhi Shoshone on August 13, 1805, the first time the flag was unfurled in present-day Idaho.

moments.title: Lemhi Pass
moments.text: The Shoshone called it We-yah-vee, and later the Salmon to Red Rock stage crossed it, twelve hours for eight dollars, until the railroad went over Bannock Pass in 1910.

moments.title: Horseshoe Bend Creek
moments.text: Just below the pass, Lewis and his men drank from this creek and took comfort that its water, at least, would reach the Columbia.

practical: Single-lane gravel with grades near 20 percent and a 4,000-foot climb and descent; allow at least three hours. Buses, RVs and trailers are not recommended on the Agency Creek Road, whose first two miles below the pass are steep, narrow and blind-cornered. The road is normally free of snow from early June through October.
